LD 2000: An Act to Amend the Laws Governing Qualifying Contributions of Cash Under the Maine Clean Election Act

My name is Alison Smith, and I'm testifying as a volunteer on behalf of Maine Citizens for Clean Elections.
Maine Citizens for Clean Elections is a nonpartisan nonprofit organization working to ensure that Maine's campaign finance laws, elections, and government serve the public interest, both in principle and in practice.
We wish to address the asterisked note in the testimony of Jonathan Wayne, Executive Director of Maine's Ethics Commission, regarding the reporting of independent expenditures in the final days of a campaign.
MCCE appreciates the work done by the stakeholder group to identify ways to improve disclosure laws and reduce confusion and duplication for those engaged in campaign finance reporting, but we think it is a mistake to eliminate 24-hour reports in the final 6 days of an election.
Between raising the threshold for reporting from $250 to $1,000 and moving to a 48-hour requirement, we feel that the loss of transparency in the crucial final days of an election is too great. Voters must know who is behind campaign messages, and our laws and reporting requirements must support that important value. We recommend that the current 24-hour reporting requirement remain in place in the final 6 days of an election.
Thank you for your consideration.

January 21, 2026

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and distinguished members of the committee: my name is Jonathan Wayne, and I am the Executive Director of the Maine Ethics Commission. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of L.D. 2000, which is the product of an informal working group convened by the Ethics Commission to see if the deadlines for candidates, PACs, and others could be simplified in the final two weeks before an election. The working group idea was proposed by an attorney who represents candidates and PACs before the Commission when they file campaign finance reports late. The concept resonated with Commission members because these late filers regularly complain that they found the deadlines confusing.
Affected laws. The bill modifies two types of disclosure laws that are sometimes confused:

24-Hour Reports
Independent Expenditure Reports

Who files? Candidates, PACs, party committees, ballot question committees Mostly PACs and political parties; also individuals occasionally

What do they report? Large contributions received or expenditures made in the 13 days before an election Costs of ads or mailers advocating for/against candidates

Purpose of report The public and election participants should have a way to know about these large transactions before an election.
Spender confirms the communications were made independently of candidates. Reports also disclose spending to influence specific candidates.

Process. The working group met publicly twice in April and June 2025. Commissioner Dennis Marble chaired the group. Other participants were State Rep. Ann Matlack, State Rep. Benjamin Hymes, attorneys Joshua Tardy and Lisa Prosienski, former candidate Leo Kenney, and Anna Kellar from Democracy Maine. After the working group agreed on a proposal, the Ethics Commission members considered it and endorsed submitting it to the Legislature.

Some policy considerations received by the working group and the Commission: � The attached factsheet provides the specifics of the proposal. The overall objective is to
simplify the reporting obligations for candidates, PACs, and others during the last 13 or 14 days before an election when candidates and party activists are at their busiest trying to communicate with voters. � In the last two weeks before an election, LD 2000 would provide candidates and committees that must file a 24-Hour Report one additional day of breathing room to file the report. The report would be due within 48 hours after receiving a large contribution or making a large expenditure, instead of the current 24 hours. � This change would return the law back to 2004, when the Legislature changed the 48-hour deadline to 24 hours to promote the prompt disclosure of last-minute campaign activity that would affect matching funds paid to Maine Clean Election Act candidates to keep them on an even playing field. P.L. 2003, Chapter 628. (Matching funds are no longer part of the Maine Clean Election Act program.) � LD 2000 as written would also provide PACs, parties and others filing Independent Expenditure reports one additional day to file the report within the last 13 days before an election. Please note the Commission ran out of time to fully resolve this deadline as it relates to the last six days before the election (see note at the end of the factsheet). � LD 2000 would increase the transaction amounts that require 24-Hour and Independent Expenditure reports. In other words, the threshold amount for what is considered a "large" transaction that must be disclosed before the election would be increased. � Our research indicates that the $1,000 spending threshold that would require candidates and referendum groups to file a 24-Hour Report was the same in 1983 as it is today. That threshold may be overdue for an increase. (At that time, the report was due in 48 hours.) � The working group concluded that the threshold amounts requiring 24-Hour Reports by candidates could vary depending on which office the candidate is seeking. The bill has been written as emergency legislation in case the Legislature would like it to take effect in this year's primary and general elections. The Commission sees no problem administering the proposed requirements in 2026. Thank you for your consideration of this testimony.

Unallocated Language to Address IT Problems that Disadvantaged Some Maine Clean Election Act Candidates
In addition, I would like to propose that unallocated language be added to LD 2000 that would extend the time for some candidates to qualify for Maine Clean Election Act (MCEA) funding. This seems necessary because of the unexpectedly long period of time it took our IT vendor to convert campaign finance information from our old database/eFiling system to our new system.
For 28 days beginning on January 15, 2026, dozens of candidates wished to register with our office but could not register online in our eFiling system. Moreover, these candidates could not use the Commission's online qualifying contribution service to receive qualifying contributions by credit card. Many of these candidates delayed registering altogether. The 28-day delay represents 25% or more of the time these candidates will have to qualify for MCEA funding this year. This is a significant reduction in the time they have to qualify.
I believe this delay by the Commission's IT vendor has resulted in an unfair situation in which 2/3 of our MCEA candidates have enjoyed the regular opportunity to qualify for public funds, but the other 1/3 of MCEA candidates have a significantly diminished period to qualify. I therefore recommend the following unallocated language:
For legislative candidates seeking Maine Clean Election Act funding in 2026 who registered with the Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices after January 15, 2026, notwithstanding the definition of "qualifying period" in the Maine Revised Statutes, Title 21-A, section 1122, subsection 8, the qualifying period is extended for those candidates until May 21, 2026. This represents a 28-day extension for candidates who registered with our office after January 15, 2026. Thank you for your consideration of this amendment.

The committees of political parties qualified under section 301 shall file campaign finance reports on forms prescribed by the commission as required by this section.
1. Contributions. A party committee shall report all contributions in cash or in kind from a single contributor that in the aggregate total more than $200. The party committee shall report the name, mailing address, occupation and place of business of each contributor. 21-A M.R.S. � 1052. Definitions
As used in this subchapter, unless the context otherwise indicates, the following terms have the following meanings.
1. Campaign. "Campaign" means any course of activities to influence the nomination or election of a candidate or to initiate or influence any of the following ballot measures:
A. A people's veto referendum under the Constitution of Maine, Article IV, Part Third, Section 17;
B. A direct initiative of legislation under the Constitution of Maine, Article IV, Part Third, Section 18;
C. An amendment to the Constitution of Maine under Article X, Section 4;

D. A referendum vote on a measure enacted by the Legislature and expressly conditioned upon ratification by a referendum vote under the Constitution of Maine, Article IV, Part Third, Section 19;
E. The ratification of the issue of bonds by the State or any agency thereof; and
F. Any county or municipal referendum.
2. Committee. "Committee" means any political action committee or ballot question committee and includes any agent of a political action committee or ballot question committee.
2-A. Ballot question committee. "Ballot question committee" means a person that receives contributions or makes expenditures aggregating in excess of $5,000 for the purpose of initiating or influencing a campaign, other than a campaign for the nomination or election of a candidate. The term "ballot question committee" does not include a political action committee or an exempt donor.Party committees and exempt donors do not need to register as ballot question committees. A political action committee is exempt from registering as a ballot question committee if it meets the requirements for the exception in section 1052-A, subsection 1-A, paragraph A.

Unallocated Language
For legislative candidates seeking Maine Clean Election Act funding in 2026 who registered with the Maine Commission on Governmental Ethics and Election Practices after January 15, 2026, notwithstanding the definition of "qualifying period" in the Maine Revised Statutes, Title 21-A, section 1122, subsection 8, the qualifying period is extended for those candidates until May 21, 2026.
SUMMARY
The amendment clarifies that party committees must disclose in their campaign finance reports the amounts they have spent to support or oppose candidates or ballot questions. The amendment adds party committees to the list of entities that are exempt from the definition of ballot question committee. The amendment also extends the qualifying period by 28 days for legislative candidates seeking Maine Clean Election Act funding who registered after January 15, 2026 and were therefore disadvantaged by problems in the database systems of the Maine Ethics Commission. This represents about one-third of the legislative candidates expected to participate in the Maine Clean Election Act program in 2026.
